title: Taylor Swift - Tidy Tuesday 2
text:
The world has grown up along side Taylor Swift, and with that, her music has changed. Here is a visualization of her songs relationship to loudness and danceability. Each point represents a song and each color represents one of her albums. This data set was made in 2023 so it includes her songs and albums up to that date.

ggplot(Taylor_Swift, aes(x = loudness, y = danceability, color = album_name))+
  geom_point()+
  scale_color_taylor_d() +
  labs(x = "Loudness", y="Danceability", title = "Taylor Swift Danceability", color = "Album")

title: Pixar Movies - Tidy Tuesday 1
text:
Everyone loves a good Pixar movie. You go as a kid, you go as a parent, you go as a college student who misses the innocence and nostalgia that Pixar movies inspire. But why does it feel like every movie is so darn long these days? Let’s explore that through a plot.

pixar_data <- pixar_films |>
  left_join(public_response, by = "film")


ggplot(pixar_data, aes(x = release_date, y = run_time))+
  geom_point()+
  labs(x = "Release Date", y="Run Time min", title = "Pixar Films Release Date and Run Times")










Data for this visualization was accessed through the TidyTuesday Pixar Films dataset.
Original data:
Leung, Eric. pixarfilms: An R Data Package to Explore Pixar Films, the People, and Reception Data. Data provided mostly in part by Wikipedia.

title: Netflix Data Analysis
text:
Netflix Media with Murder
For this graph, I wanted to look at the content ratings of movies and TV shows on Netflix that mention murder or killing in their descriptions. I filtered the data to include descriptions containing the words “murder,” “kill,” or “killed.” I then made a bar graph to compare how many movies and TV shows fall into each rating category. I was interested in seeing whether media that mentions murder tends to have more mature ratings and whether there is a difference between movies and TV shows.


Show Code
netflix_titles <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2021/2021-04-20/netflix_titles.csv')
netflix_titles <- netflix_titles|>
  mutate(rating_fct = fct_relevel(factor(rating),  "G", "TV-Y", "TV-G", "TV-Y7", "TV-Y7-FV",
"PG", "TV-PG", "PG-13", "TV-14",
"R", "TV-MA", "NC-17"))|>
  mutate( decade = floor(release_year / 10) * 10)
murder <- netflix_titles|>
  filter(str_detect(description, regex("murder|\\bkill(ed)?\\b", ignore_case = TRUE)))




Show Code
murder|>
  ggplot(aes(y = rating_fct))+
  geom_bar(fill = "#B0CCFF")+
  facet_wrap(~type, scales = "free_x")+
  labs(title = "Netflix Media with Murder", x = "Number", y = "Rating")+
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Helvetica Neue")+
theme_light()+
theme(
  text = element_text(size = 14, color = "#263D69")
)+
theme(
  strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#263D69", color = NA),
  strip.text = element_text(size = 14, color = "#FFEBE8")
)











American Comedies by Decade
For this graph, I looked at American comedy movies on Netflix and which decades they were released in. I chose a list of famous comedy actors, including Adam Sandler, Jim Carrey, and Amy Pohler, and used their names to see which movies featured at least one of these actors. I then made a bar graph to compare the number of comedies released in each decade and how many featured someone from my list. I wanted to see whether famous comedy actors appeared more frequently in certain decades and how the number of American comedies changed over time.


Show Code
comedies <- netflix_titles|>
  filter(type == "Movie", str_detect(country, "United States"),
    str_detect(listed_in, "Comedies"))

 
comedies <- comedies |>
  mutate(
    famous_actor = str_detect(
      cast, "\\b(Adam Sandler|Jim Carrey|Will Ferrell|Ben Stiller|Eddie Murphy|Steve Carell|Seth Rogen|Jonah Hill|Paul Rudd|Kevin Hart|Jack Black|Melissa McCarthy|Kristen Wiig|Tina Fey|Amy Poehler|Maya Rudolph|Tiffany Haddish|Jennifer Aniston|Sandra Bullock|Julia Roberts)(?=,|$)"
      ))
    
  
  comedies |>
  ggplot(aes(x = decade, fill = famous_actor)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("TRUE" = "#263D69", "FALSE" = "#B0CCFF"),
    labels = c("FALSE" = "No", "TRUE" = "Yes"),
    name = "Contains Famous Comedy Actor"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "American Comedies by Release Year",
    x = "Decade",
    y = "Number of Movies"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Helvetica Neue")+
theme_light()+
theme(
  text = element_text(size = 9, color = "#263D69")
)











Romantic Comedy
For this graph, I made a data table of all movies that were listed in the categories “Romantic Movies” and “Comedies” to find the romcoms, I then looked in the descriptions of the movie to see which used male pronouns and female pronouns. I also looked at the titles to see which one used some variation of the word love.


Show Code
romcom <- netflix_titles|>
  filter(type == "Movie", str_detect(listed_in, "Comedies"))|>
  filter(str_detect(listed_in, "Romantic Movies"))|>
 mutate(female = str_count(description, regex("\\b(she|her|hers)\\b", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
mutate(male = str_count(description, regex("\\b(him|he|his)\\b", ignore_case = TRUE)))|>
mutate(love = str_extract(title, regex("\\b(love|lover|loved)\\b", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
mutate(love = if_else(!is.na(love), "Love", "No Love"))

  romcom |>
  ggplot(aes(x = male, y = female, color = love)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.5, height = 0.5, size = 2.5) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "#263D69") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Love" = "#263D69", "No Love" = "#B0CCFF"),
    name = "Love in Title"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Gendered Pronouns in Romantic Comedies",
    x = "Male Pronouns",
    y = "Female Pronouns"
  ) +
  theme_light(base_family = "Helvetica Neue") +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 14, color = "#263D69")
  )











About the Data
For this project, I used the Netflix Titles dataset from TidyTuesday (April 20, 2021). The original dataset was shared on Kaggle by Shivam Bansal and contains information about movies and TV shows available on Netflix, including their titles, genres, cast members, release years, content ratings, and descriptions.
Source: TidyTuesday Netflix Dataset

title: Does Chocolate Win Halloween?
text:
I have always thought that the best candies contain chocolate and peanuts, but in this analysis I am focusing on chocolate alone. I am using FiveThirtyEight’s dataset of 85 candies, which records their ingredients and their win percentages in head-to-head online candy matchups. I want to know whether candies containing chocolate have a higher average win percentage than candies without chocolate. To investigate this question, I will compare the original group means and run a permutation test that simulates the null hypothesis of no relationship between chocolate content and win percentage.
Research question: Do chocolate candies have a higher average win percentage than non-chocolate candies?

Null hypothesis: Chocolate content and win percentage are unrelated.
Alternative hypothesis: Chocolate candies have a higher average win percentage.
Test statistic: Mean win percentage for chocolate candies minus mean win percentage for non-chocolate candies (in percentage points).

Alternative hypothesis: Chocolate candies have a higher average win percentage.

title: Does Chocolate Win Halloween?
text:
Original data


Show R code
library(tidyverse)

candy <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fivethirtyeight/data/master/candy-power-ranking/candy-data.csv"
) |>
  mutate(chocolate = if_else(chocolate == 1, "Yes", "No"))

candy |>
  select(competitorname, chocolate, winpercent) |>
  head()


# A tibble: 6 × 3
  competitorname chocolate winpercent
  <chr>          <chr>          <dbl>
1 100 Grand      Yes             67.0
2 3 Musketeers   Yes             67.6
3 One dime       No              32.3
4 One quarter    No              46.1
5 Air Heads      No              52.3
6 Almond Joy     Yes             50.3


Each row represents one candy. The chocolate variable tells us whether the candy contains chocolate, and winpercent is the percentage of head-to-head matchups in which the candy was chosen.
First, I visualize the original data with a boxplot. The individual points represent candies, and the yellow diamonds show the means that I will compare in my permutation test.


Show R code
candy |>
  ggplot(aes(x = chocolate, y = winpercent, fill = chocolate)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.48,
    alpha = 0.75,
    outlier.shape = NA
  ) +
  geom_jitter(
    width = 0.13,
    alpha = 0.6,
    color = "#2A0081"
  ) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "point",
    shape = 23,
    size = 4,
    fill = "#F9C45C",
    color = "#2A0081"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("No" = "#D8C7F2", "Yes" = "#F4A6C6"),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Chocolate and Candy Popularity",
    subtitle = "Each point is one candy; yellow diamonds mark group means",
    x = "Contains chocolate",
    y = "Head-to-head matchups won (%)",
    caption = "Data: FiveThirtyEight candy power ranking"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      color = "#401465"
    )
  )









To measure the observed gap, I calculate the mean win percentage of each group and subtract the non-chocolate mean from the chocolate mean.


Show R code
group_means <- candy |>
  group_by(chocolate) |>
  summarize(
    mean_win = mean(winpercent),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

group_means


# A tibble: 2 × 2
  chocolate mean_win
  <chr>        <dbl>
1 No            42.1
2 Yes           60.9


Show R code
observed_diff <- candy |>
  summarize(
    diff = mean(winpercent[chocolate == "Yes"]) -
           mean(winpercent[chocolate == "No"])
  ) |>
  pull(diff)

observed_diff


[1] 18.77927








NoteObserved difference



Chocolate candies have a mean win percentage of 60.9%, compared with 42.1% for non-chocolate candies.
The difference is 18.8 percentage points in favor of chocolate candies.

title: Does Chocolate Win Halloween?
Does Chocolate Win Halloween?
text:
Null permutation distribution
The histogram shows all 5,000 simulated differences in means. If the null hypothesis is true, I would expect the simulated differences to cluster around zero.
The dashed pink line shows the observed difference from the original candy data, so we can see whether it is unusually large relative to the null distribution.


Show R code
simulations |>
  ggplot(aes(x = diff)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 30,
    fill = "#2A0081",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = observed_diff,
    color = "#D62F8B",
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Null Distribution of Candy Win Percentages",
    subtitle = "5,000 permutations under the null hypothesis",
    x = "Difference in mean win percentage (Yes - No), percentage points",
    y = "Number of simulations",
    caption = "Dashed pink line = observed difference"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      color = "#2A0081"
    )
  )









Because my alternative hypothesis predicts a higher win percentage for chocolate candies, I use a right-tailed p-value. This is the proportion of simulations whose difference is greater than or equal to the observed difference.


Show R code
p_value <- simulations |>
  summarize(p = mean(diff >= observed_diff)) |>
  pull(p)

extreme_count <- sum(simulations$diff >= observed_diff)

p_value


[1] 0


Show R code
extreme_count


[1] 0








ImportantPermutation test result



0 out of 5,000 simulated differences were at least as large as the observed difference of 18.8 percentage points.
The simulated right-tail proportion was 0.
Because no simulations were as extreme, I report p < 0.0002 to reflect the simulation’s resolution; this does not mean the true p-value is exactly zero.

title: Does Chocolate Win Halloween?
text:
Conclusion
The original data show that chocolate candies have a higher mean win percentage than candies without chocolate, with an observed difference of 18.8 percentage points.
I wrote a function that shuffles win percentages and used map_dbl() to repeat it 5,000 times, creating a null distribution for the difference in means.
None of those simulations produced a difference as large as the observed one, providing strong evidence of an association between chocolate content and win percentage in this dataset.
Because the candies and the online participants were not randomly sampled from all candies and consumers, I cannot generalize this result to everyone or claim that chocolate causes a candy to be more popular.

The original data come from Walt Hickey’s The Ultimate Halloween Candy Power Ranking for FiveThirtyEight, based on online head-to-head candy preference matchups.
